newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's Khatami adopts low-key style in first days.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Khatami adopts low-key style in first days.

text.p: Iranian President Mohammad Khatami, who submitted his cabinet choices to parliament on Tuesday, has adopted a low-key approach in his first days of office despite winning a landslide election victory in May.

Since his inauguration last week, the 54-year-old moderate Shi'ite cleric has rarely been seen in public and has scarcely appeared on state-run television, used extensively by his predecessors and the ruling clerical establishment.

Government buildings, banks and hotels are now starting to hang large framed portraits of Khatami next to the standard photos of revolutionary founder Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini and supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Arriving at Tehran's Mehrabad international airport, a visitor could have no idea that Iran had a new president, the highest elected official in the country of 60 million people.
"There is going to be no cult of personality around Khatami. He wants to be seen as a competent personality who can bring changes to people's lives," said one diplomat.

Khatami has held no formal news conference to outline his plans since being sworn into office despite high expectations of millions of Iranians who swept him into power based on his reputation as a moderate who would press for more freedoms.
The middle-level clergyman won nearly 70 percent, or 20 million, of the popular vote, in the May election.
Outgoing president Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and Khatami's defeated election opponent, parliamentary speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, still have higher media profiles.
A photo call on Khatami's first working day in office showed him dining with his fellow workers at the presidential office staff cafeteria eating a simple meal of chicken and rice.
Khatami used the occasion of receiving official blessing for his presidency from Khamenei to cite lines from the 14th-century Persian poet Hafiz.

He has also discouraged newspapers from printing lengthy letters in his praise and was expected, according to some press accounts, to appoint a woman to his cabinet -- a first for Iran since the 1979 revolution. But the list of ministers submitted to parliament on Tuesday was exclusively male.
"Khatami is not charging into office. There is not going to be any famous first 100 days in power. It is going to be a slow, drawn-out game to overcome his opponents," one diplomat said.
Khatami is facing his sternest political task in his attempt to get the conservative-dominated parliament to accept his nominations for cabinet posts, diplomats say.
Deputies begin three five-hour sessions on the merits of his ministers next Tuesday.

Iranian newspapers reported that Khatami had come under pressure over his cabinet from various factions in parliament and that he might have to accept compromise candidates particularly over such key ministries as foreign affairs, intelligence (internal security), culture and interior.
